title: Should you give positive feedback?
author: Luca Foppoli
summary: Luca Foppoli argues that managers should give positive feedback, because managerial advice neglects it in favor of the harder negative conversation. He gives two reasons: it reinforces the desired behaviors, so people do not perform well on one project and flounder on the next, and it raises motivation, enthusiasm and ownership because people appreciate being appreciated. He answers the objection that good work is what the salary pays for by saying the salary buys the what, while only the manager can say whether the how was right. Vague praise such as 'Great job' does not count as feedback. He recommends the same four-part structure used for negative feedback, observation, feeling, need and request, with preparation, and he illustrates it with a product-launch stakeholder example. His closing frame is that negative feedback is for when the how is wrong and positive feedback for when the how is right.
points: Positive feedback reinforces specific behaviors, so a person who is never told what was right may repeat it on one project and lose it on the next.
Praise also raises motivation and ownership, and leaders who pretend not to need appreciation are playing a status game.
A salary pays for the what in the job description, but only explicit feedback tells people whether the how met the manager's standard.
Phrases such as 'Great job' or 'Keep it up' are not feedback; use observation, feeling, need and request.
Unprepared praise either rambles and dents a leader's calm image or sends a confused message that conveys only happiness.
quotes: Coaching is the single most powerful lever to drive performance and feedback is a crucial piece of it.
If people ignore whether they have done something right, you risk them performing well on project 1 and floundering on project 2.
You are human and humans appreciate being appreciated: do this to your team and see their motivation go up, and with it their enthusiasm, sense of ownership and desire to make things happen.
The salary pays for the what, found in a job description that was outdated on day 2, but the real differentiator is how that what gets done.
Spoiler alert: “Great job!”, “Congratulations”, “Keep it up!” are not examples of positive feedback.
After every such interaction I found myself trusting you more, to the point that I stopped checking your work.
Negative feedback is what you use when the how is wrong. Positive feedback is what you use when the how is right.
